Helm and Kubernetes fundamentals — Beginner

001What is Helm in Kubernetes?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm version
helm list -A

Final interview-ready answer

Helm is a package manager that turns a reusable chart into Kubernetes manifests. It installs and updates a named release through the Kubernetes API. Instead of copying ten YAML files for every environment, I maintain one chart and change its values. Kubernetes, not Helm, runs the containers.

002Why do we need Helm? What problems does it solve?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml

Final interview-ready answer

Helm reduces repeated YAML, makes application configuration consistent and records release revisions for upgrades and rollback. It does not replace Kubernetes or automatically guarantee availability. I use it for microservices and platform components with repeatable settings.

003What is a Helm chart?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm create orders-api
helm show chart ./orders-api

Final interview-ready answer

A chart is a directory containing Chart.yaml, values.yaml and templates, optionally dependencies, CRDs and a schema. It describes an application package, not a running container. The templates produce Kubernetes objects when supplied with values.

004What is a Helm release?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm list -A
helm status orders -n orders-dev

Final interview-ready answer

A release is a named installation of a chart in a namespace, with revision history. The same chart can be installed as orders-dev and orders-qa with different settings. A release can be failed or pending, not necessarily running.

005What is a Helm repository and where are charts stored?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm repo list
helm search hub prometheus

Final interview-ready answer

A classic repository serves chart archives and index.yaml over HTTP(S). Teams may store chart source in Git and publish packages to a private repository or OCI registry. Artifact Hub is a discovery catalog, not itself the chart repository.

006Explain Helm architecture and how it works.

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm env
kubectl -n orders-dev get secrets -l owner=helm

Final interview-ready answer

With Helm 3, the client reads a chart and overrides, renders Go templates, authenticates using kubeconfig and sends objects to the Kubernetes API. The default release storage uses Kubernetes Secrets in the release namespace. Controllers then create Pods and endpoints.

007What is the difference between Helm 2, Helm 3 and Helm 4?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

AspectHelm 2Helm 3 / 4
ServerTillerNo Tiller
AuthorizationTiller identityClient identity
Chart formatv1 commonv2 common

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm version
helm upgrade --help

Final interview-ready answer

Helm 2 used the in-cluster Tiller service. Helm 3 removed Tiller and uses the client's Kubernetes permissions. Helm 4 retains a Tiller-free architecture but introduces changes such as server-side apply support and different flags. These labs target Helm 3; check help and migration notes for Helm 4.

008What is the difference between Helm and kubectl apply?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

Aspectkubectl applyDirect Helm
InputManifestsChart + values
HistoryNo Helm revisionsRelease revisions
RollbackGit / controller-specifichelm rollback

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f rendered.yaml

Final interview-ready answer

kubectl apply sends declarative manifests to Kubernetes and does not create Helm release history. Helm renders a parameterized chart, tracks releases and offers rollback by revision. Both rely on Kubernetes for reconciliation and resource health.

009What is the difference between Helm and Kustomize?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

AspectHelmKustomize
InputTemplates and valuesBase and overlays
Release lifecycleDirect Helm supportsNone
GitOpsSupportedSupported

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl kustomize overlays/dev
helm template orders ./orders-api

Final interview-ready answer

Helm generates resources with templates and values and can manage release history. Kustomize transforms base YAML using patches and overlays without Go templates. Choose based on packaging and configuration needs; either can be rendered by GitOps tools.

010What is the difference between Helm and Argo CD?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

AspectDirect HelmArgo CD with Helm
RolePackage + release operationsContinuous GitOps reconciliation
RenderHelm CLIRepo-server uses Helm
Release historyHelm revisionsArgo CD history / Git
DriftNo continuous reconciliationDetects; optional self-heal
Rollbackhelm rollbackGit revert and sync

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm list -n orders-dev
argocd app get orders-dev

Final interview-ready answer

Helm packages and renders resources and, when used directly, manages release operations. Argo CD continuously compares desired manifests with cluster state and syncs them according to policy. When Argo CD uses Helm, it renders charts rather than installing a conventional Helm release. I roll back GitOps workloads through Git, not helm rollback. Direct Helm is a command-driven deployment mechanism; Argo CD is a long-running controller. The two can be used for different workloads, never competing ownership.

011How are Docker, ECR, Kubernetes, Helm, Jenkins and Argo CD connected?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
docker build -t orders-api:lab-v1 .
helm template orders ./orders-api

Final interview-ready answer

CI builds and scans the application image, pushes it to ECR and proposes a new image reference in Git. Helm transforms values into Deployment, Service and Ingress manifests. Either direct Helm or Argo CD applies them; kubelet pulls the image. Do not let both tools own the same resources.

Prerequisites and chart structure — Beginner

012What are the prerequisites for Helm on EKS?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
aws sts get-caller-identity
kubectl cluster-info
helm version

Final interview-ready answer

I need an existing Kubernetes cluster, a supported Helm client, kubectl, AWS CLI for EKS access, kubeconfig, network reachability and permissions to manage target resources. An EC2 admin machine is optional. For the sample app I also need an ECR image and an ingress controller if exposing HTTP.

013How do you install Helm on a Linux administration server?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
uname -m
sha256sum helm-v3.VERSION-linux-amd64.tar.gz
tar -xzf helm-v3.VERSION-linux-amd64.tar.gz
sudo install linux-amd64/helm /usr/local/bin/helm
helm version

Final interview-ready answer

Install a trusted, pinned Helm 3 binary or package for the correct OS and CPU, verify its published checksum, and add it to PATH. Helm does not need a separate server pod. Confirm the version and client environment before connecting to a cluster.

014How do you connect to an EKS cluster before using Helm?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
aws eks update-kubeconfig --region ap-south-1 --name demo-eks
kubectl config current-context
kubectl get nodes
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n orders-dev

Final interview-ready answer

I authenticate to AWS using a role or approved profile, update kubeconfig for the correct region and cluster, and verify context and authorization. An EKS private endpoint needs network connectivity from the administration machine. Never assume the default context is production.

015How do you create a Helm chart from scratch?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm create orders-api
find orders-api -maxdepth 2 -type f
helm lint orders-api

Final interview-ready answer

helm create generates a starter chart including sample templates and values. I remove unused starter templates or adapt them as a coherent set, then write my actual resource requirements and run lint/render before installing.

016Explain the Helm chart repository folder structure.

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
tree orders-api
Git repository structure
platform-gitops/
├── charts/
│   └── orders-api/
│       ├── Chart.yaml
│       ├── values.yaml
│       ├── values-dev.yaml
│       ├── values-qa.yaml
│       ├── values-prod.yaml
│       ├── values.schema.json
│       └── templates/
│           ├── _helpers.tpl
│           ├── deployment.yaml
│           ├── service.yaml
│           └── ingress.yaml
└── applications/
    ├── orders-dev.yaml
    └── orders-prod.yaml

Final interview-ready answer

Chart.yaml is metadata, values.yaml defaults, templates renders objects, charts holds dependencies, crds contains initial CRDs, and values.schema.json can validate inputs. A reusable chart may live in a dedicated Git repository with environment overrides in GitOps Git.

017What is Chart.yaml? Explain its fields.

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm show chart ./orders-api
Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: orders-api
description: Reusable Spring Boot orders API chart
type: application
version: 1.0.0
appVersion: "1.0.0"

Final interview-ready answer

Chart.yaml describes the package using apiVersion v2, name, description, type, version and optional appVersion, dependencies and kubeVersion. version identifies the chart artifact and follows SemVer. appVersion is informational unless templates use it explicitly.

018What is values.yaml?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm show values ./orders-api
helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml
values.yaml
replicaCount: 2
image:
  repository: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api
  tag: lab-v1
  digest: ""
containerPort: 8080
service:
  port: 80
ingress:
  enabled: false
  className: nginx
  host: orders-dev.example.com
healthPath: /actuator/health
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 512Mi

Final interview-ready answer

values.yaml supplies default inputs such as replicaCount, image repository, image tag, service port and ingress host. Values only affect resources when a template actually references them. I keep non-secret defaults in Git and override environment settings separately.

019What is the templates directory?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
ls orders-api/templates
helm template orders ./orders-api

Final interview-ready answer

It contains Go templates that generate Kubernetes objects. Helm uses the same values and release context across templates. A Deployment can read image and replica values while Service and Ingress read ports and hostname; their names and selectors must agree.

020What is _helpers.tpl?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api --show-only templates/service.yaml
_helpers.tpl
{{- define "orders.name" -}}
{{- .Release.Name -}}
{{- end -}}
{{- define "orders.selectorLabels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name | quote }}
{{- end -}}

Final interview-ready answer

It defines named reusable templates for resource names, common labels and selectors. Files prefixed with an underscore are helpers rather than standalone manifests. I use include with nindent to reuse labels consistently across Deployment and Service.

021What is the Helm Go template engine?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api --debug

Final interview-ready answer

It evaluates expressions like .Values.image.tag and control structures such as if, range and with. The output must be valid Kubernetes YAML. The engine does not automatically infer which variables belong in which resource.

022What is the difference between chart version, appVersion, image tag and release revision?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

VersionExampleMeaning
chart version1.0.0Chart package
appVersion1.0.0Informational metadata
image taglab-v1Registry reference
revision2Release operation

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm show chart ./orders-api
helm history orders -n orders-dev

Final interview-ready answer

Chart version identifies package changes. appVersion describes the application, image tag or digest selects the actual container, and release revision increments for Helm release operations. They need not match; an image digest is the strongest identity for promotion.

Release operations and essential commands — Beginner

023How do you install a Helm chart?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm install orders ./orders-api -n orders-dev --create-namespace -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --wait --timeout 5m

Final interview-ready answer

I create or confirm the namespace, select the chart and environment values, render and review it, then run helm install. Kubernetes schedules the resulting workloads; --wait can detect readiness problems but is not an end-to-end business test.

024How do you upgrade a Helm release?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm upgrade orders ./orders-api -n orders-dev -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --set-string image.tag=lab-v2 --wait --timeout 5m

Final interview-ready answer

Use helm upgrade with the target chart and explicit values files. Review changes and keep the same release name and namespace. Kubernetes performs the actual workload update, and Helm records a new revision. Confirm rollout and HTTP health afterward.

025What is helm rollback and how does it work?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm history orders -n orders-dev
helm rollback orders 1 -n orders-dev --wait --timeout 5m

Final interview-ready answer

Helm uses a previous release revision's stored manifest and configuration to update managed resources. Rollback creates another revision; it does not erase history or undo database migrations. Confirm the desired known-good version and test application health afterward.

026What is the difference between helm install, upgrade and rollback?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

CommandActionResult
installInitial deploymentRevision 1
upgradeModify releaseNew revision
rollbackRestore old revisionNew revision

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm history orders -n orders-dev
helm status orders -n orders-dev

Final interview-ready answer

Install creates a release, upgrade changes a release, and rollback restores a prior revision as a new operation. The release name and namespace identify the target. Use history and status to confirm what actually happened.

027What is helm upgrade --install?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm upgrade --install orders ./orders-api -n orders-dev --create-namespace -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --wait --timeout 5m

Final interview-ready answer

It selects install when a release does not exist and upgrade when it does. It is convenient for repeatable CI commands, but repeated runs can create revisions or execute hooks, so it is not a guarantee of no side effects.

028How do you list releases, check status and view history?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm list -A
helm status orders -n orders-dev
helm history orders -n orders-dev
Illustrative output — not a live command result
$ helm list -n orders-dev
NAME     NAMESPACE    REVISION  STATUS    CHART             APP VERSION
orders   orders-dev   1         deployed  orders-api-1.0.0  1.0.0

Final interview-ready answer

Use helm list to locate the release, helm status for its current release state and helm history for previous revisions. Include the namespace. A deployed release status is not proof that users can reach the application.

029How do you uninstall a Helm release?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm get manifest orders -n orders-dev
helm uninstall orders -n orders-dev --dry-run

Final interview-ready answer

helm uninstall removes the release's managed resources and normally deletes its history. --keep-history preserves the history record, not application data. CRDs, retained resources or PVCs can have separate lifecycles; inspect them first.

030What is helm repo add, repo update and helm search?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
helm search repo prometheus-community --versions

Final interview-ready answer

Add registers a named classic repository, update refreshes its cached index and search repo finds charts locally from those indexes. Search hub discovers charts through Artifact Hub. OCI registries do not use helm repo add.

031What is helm show and helm pull?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm show values prometheus-community/prometheus --version VERSION
helm pull prometheus-community/prometheus --version VERSION

Final interview-ready answer

helm show displays chart metadata, defaults, README or CRDs without installing. helm pull downloads a selected package for inspection or controlled distribution. Pin a version rather than blindly choosing the newest chart.

032What is helm lint?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm lint ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --strict

Final interview-ready answer

Lint checks chart structure and rendering-related issues before release. It is an early validation step, not proof that the target cluster supports every API or that pods start. Use the same values as the intended deployment.

033What is helm template? How is it different from helm install?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

CommandCluster mutationOutput
helm templateNoRendered YAML
helm installYesRelease and resources

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api -n orders-dev -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml > rendered.yaml
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -n orders-dev -f rendered.yaml

Final interview-ready answer

helm template generates YAML for review without creating a Helm release. Install renders and sends resources to Kubernetes. Local rendering may not reflect live API capabilities or lookup results; validate against the target cluster too.

034What is helm get values vs helm get manifest?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

CommandOutput
helm get valuesUser-supplied overrides
helm get values -aComputed values
helm get manifestStored rendered resources
kubectl get -o yamlLive object

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm get values orders -n orders-dev -a
helm get manifest orders -n orders-dev

Final interview-ready answer

helm get values returns supplied overrides by default; -a returns computed values. helm get manifest returns the stored rendered manifest, not necessarily current live objects. Compare with kubectl get when investigating drift. Both may expose secrets.

035What are the essential Helm commands?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm version
helm list -A
helm lint ./orders-api
helm template orders ./orders-api
helm history orders -n orders-dev

Final interview-ready answer

I use version and repo commands for setup, lint/template for validation, install/upgrade for deployment, list/status/history/get for inspection, test for runtime checks, rollback for recovery and uninstall for approved removal. Namespace and chart version matter in every operation.

Connected chart deployment lab — Intermediate

036How do you write a complete values.yaml for a microservice?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm show values ./orders-api
values.yaml
replicaCount: 2
image:
  repository: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api
  tag: lab-v1
  digest: ""
containerPort: 8080
service:
  port: 80
ingress:
  enabled: false
  className: nginx
  host: orders-dev.example.com
healthPath: /actuator/health
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 512Mi

Final interview-ready answer

I define replicas, image repository/tag, container port, Service port, Ingress host, resources and health settings as explicit inputs. Templates use these values, and a schema can catch wrong types. The sample orders-api listens on 8080 and serves /actuator/health.

037How do you write a Helm Deployment template?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api --show-only templates/deployment.yaml
templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "orders.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        {{- include "orders.selectorLabels" . | nindent 8 }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: orders-api
          {{- if .Values.image.digest }}
          image: {{ printf "%s@%s" .Values.image.repository .Values.image.digest | quote }}
          {{- else }}
          image: {{ printf "%s:%s" .Values.image.repository .Values.image.tag | quote }}
          {{- end }}
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: {{ .Values.containerPort }}
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: {{ .Values.healthPath | quote }}
              port: http
          resources:
            {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}

Final interview-ready answer

I use apps/v1 Deployment, a stable selector matching pod labels, replicaCount, image repository and tag, container port and readiness probe. Helm renders the variables, then Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers create Pods.

038How do you write a Helm Service template?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api --show-only templates/service.yaml
templates/service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    {{- include "orders.selectorLabels" . | nindent 4 }}
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: {{ .Values.service.port }}
      targetPort: http

Final interview-ready answer

The Service uses a stable name and a selector matching Pod labels. port 80 is the Service port and targetPort http points to the named container port 8080. EndpointSlices reflect the matching ready Pods.

039How do you write a Helm Ingress template?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --show-only templates/ingress.yaml
templates/ingress.yaml
{{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }}
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
spec:
  ingressClassName: {{ .Values.ingress.className | quote }}
  rules:
    - host: {{ .Values.ingress.host | quote }}
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
                port:
                  number: {{ .Values.service.port }}
{{- end }}

Final interview-ready answer

A networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress defines host, path, ingressClassName and backend Service name/port. It needs a functioning ingress controller, DNS and TLS configuration if HTTPS is required. Ingress alone does not create a working external endpoint.

040How are Deployment, Service, Ingress and values.yaml connected?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

ConnectionSourceTarget
Application imagevalues.imageDeployment container image
Pod identityDeployment selectorPod labels
TrafficService selectorMatching Pods
PortService port 80Named port http / 8080
RoutingIngress backendService orders:80

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev get deploy,svc,ingress,endpointslices
Illustrative rendered relationships
Ingress backend: orders:80
Service: orders, port 80, targetPort http
Service selector: app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-api, app.kubernetes.io/instance=orders
Pod labels: same selector labels
Container port: http = 8080

Final interview-ready answer

The same helper name connects the Ingress backend to the Service. A stable app label connects Service selector to pod labels and Deployment selector. Values set port, image and host. The user request reaches the application through the configured ingress data plane, never through Helm.

041How do you deploy a complete Helm chart to EKS and test the URL?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm upgrade --install orders ./orders-api -n orders-dev --create-namespace -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --wait
kubectl -n orders-dev rollout status deployment/orders
kubectl -n orders-dev port-forward svc/orders 8080:80

Complete connected lab — build the chart from these files

Create a clean orders-api directory with only the files below (do not retain conflicting helm create starter templates). Replace sample account and image with a real accessible image running on port 8080 and exposing /actuator/health. Ensure cluster access and a compatible ingress controller. For local verification you may leave ingress disabled. Use direct Helm OR Argo CD, not both for the same resources.

Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: orders-api
description: Reusable Spring Boot orders API chart
type: application
version: 1.0.0
appVersion: "1.0.0"
values.yaml
replicaCount: 2
image:
  repository: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api
  tag: lab-v1
  digest: ""
containerPort: 8080
service:
  port: 80
ingress:
  enabled: false
  className: nginx
  host: orders-dev.example.com
healthPath: /actuator/health
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 512Mi
values-dev.yaml
replicaCount: 2
ingress:
  enabled: true
  host: orders-dev.example.com
values-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 4
ingress:
  enabled: true
  host: orders.example.com
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: "1"
    memory: 1Gi
templates/_helpers.tpl
{{- define "orders.name" -}}
{{- .Release.Name -}}
{{- end -}}
{{- define "orders.selectorLabels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name | quote }}
{{- end -}}
templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "orders.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        {{- include "orders.selectorLabels" . | nindent 8 }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: orders-api
          {{- if .Values.image.digest }}
          image: {{ printf "%s@%s" .Values.image.repository .Values.image.digest | quote }}
          {{- else }}
          image: {{ printf "%s:%s" .Values.image.repository .Values.image.tag | quote }}
          {{- end }}
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: {{ .Values.containerPort }}
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: {{ .Values.healthPath | quote }}
              port: http
          resources:
            {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
templates/service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    {{- include "orders.selectorLabels" . | nindent 4 }}
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: {{ .Values.service.port }}
      targetPort: http
templates/ingress.yaml
{{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }}
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
spec:
  ingressClassName: {{ .Values.ingress.className | quote }}
  rules:
    - host: {{ .Values.ingress.host | quote }}
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
                port:
                  number: {{ .Values.service.port }}
{{- end }}
Terminal · direct Helm lab
helm lint ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml
helm template orders ./orders-api -n orders-dev -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml > rendered.yaml
# Review rendered.yaml before applying; namespace must exist for server dry-run.
helm upgrade --install orders ./orders-api -n orders-dev --create-namespace -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --atomic --timeout 5m
kubectl -n orders-dev rollout status deployment/orders --timeout=5m
kubectl -n orders-dev get deploy,svc,ingress,endpointslices
kubectl -n orders-dev port-forward svc/orders 8080:80
# Separate terminal: curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/actuator/health
# For GitOps alternative, use a different namespace or remove the lab release with approval first.
GitOps alternative — Application YAML
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: orders-dev
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default # Lab only; use a restricted project in production
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/example-org/platform-gitops.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: charts/orders-api
    helm:
      releaseName: orders
      valueFiles:
        - values-dev.yaml
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: orders-dev
  syncPolicy:
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true

Final interview-ready answer

After pushing the image and validating kubeconfig, I lint, render, review and install using a dev values file. I verify rollout, Service endpoints, ingress controller and DNS. Port forwarding allows a local health check even before external DNS is ready.

Go templates and configuration — Intermediate

042How do Helm values overrides and precedence work?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

PriorityInput
LowestChart defaults
HigherParent/subchart overrides
HigherValues files left to right
Highest--set family overrides

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml -f override.yaml --set-string image.tag=lab-v2
values-dev.yaml
replicaCount: 2
ingress:
  enabled: true
  host: orders-dev.example.com
values-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 4
ingress:
  enabled: true
  host: orders.example.com
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: "1"
    memory: 1Gi

Final interview-ready answer

Chart defaults are lowest, parent values can override subchart defaults, values files are applied in order and command-line set overrides take priority. Later files win for duplicate keys. Lists are generally replaced rather than merged item-by-item. Always render the exact inputs.

043What is the difference between --set, --set-string, --set-file and -f?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

FlagUse
-fStructured values file
--setInline value
--set-stringForce string
--set-fileRead file content

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --set-string image.tag=001

Final interview-ready answer

--set parses inline YAML-like values, --set-string forces a string, --set-file reads a file into a value, and -f loads a structured YAML values file. Prefer checked-in non-secret files for reproducibility; never pass secrets on command lines.

044How do you use if, else and conditional resources in Helm?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api --set ingress.enabled=false
Conditional template
{{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }}
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
spec:
  ingressClassName: {{ .Values.ingress.className | quote }}
  rules:
    - host: {{ .Values.ingress.host | quote }}
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
                port:
                  number: {{ .Values.service.port }}
{{- end }}

Final interview-ready answer

A condition can include or omit a resource based on values, such as ingress.enabled. For booleans, explicitly use true or false rather than quoted strings. Check indentation and render both enabled and disabled cases.

045How do you use range and with in Helm?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api --debug
Example environment list fragment
env:
{{- range .Values.extraEnv }}
  - name: {{ .name | quote }}
    value: {{ .value | quote }}
{{- end }}
# Input: extraEnv: [{name: LOG_LEVEL, value: INFO}]

Final interview-ready answer

range repeats a template for list or map entries. with changes the current scope to an object. Both can change what dot means, so use $ to access the root context when needed. Test empty and populated inputs.

046How do you use include, define, default, required, quote, toYaml and nindent?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm lint ./orders-api --strict
Named helper
{{- define "orders.name" -}}
{{- .Release.Name -}}
{{- end -}}
{{- define "orders.selectorLabels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name | quote }}
{{- end -}}

Final interview-ready answer

define creates helpers and include returns their text for pipelines. default supplies a fallback; required stops rendering for missing or empty values. quote protects strings and toYaml/nindent format nested structures. Use schema for types and required fields too.

047What are .Values, .Release, .Chart, .Capabilities and .Files?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

ObjectMeaning
.ValuesInputs
.ReleaseRelease context
.ChartMetadata
.CapabilitiesCluster capabilities
.FilesBundled file access

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api --kube-version 1.31.0

Final interview-ready answer

They are built-in template objects: input values, release metadata, chart metadata, Kubernetes API capability information and access to bundled chart files. Do not confuse .Chart.AppVersion with the image selected unless the template explicitly uses it.

048What is values.schema.json and why do we use it?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm lint ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml
helm template orders ./orders-api --set replicaCount=invalid
values.schema.json (minimal example)
{
  "type": "object",
  "required": [
    "replicaCount",
    "image"
  ],
  "properties": {
    "replicaCount": {
      "type": "integer",
      "minimum": 1
    },
    "image": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": [
        "repository",
        "tag"
      ],
      "properties": {
        "repository": {
          "type": "string",
          "minLength": 1
        },
        "tag": {
          "type": "string"
        },
        "digest": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Final interview-ready answer

It validates values against JSON Schema, including types, required fields and accepted ranges. This catches configuration mistakes before API submission, but does not replace Kubernetes validation or runtime tests.

049How do you create ConfigMaps and reference configuration in Helm?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev get configmaps
kubectl -n orders-dev describe deploy orders
ConfigMap fragment (add matching values and Deployment reference)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: {{ .Values.logLevel | default "INFO" | quote }}
# Deployment container envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: orders-config}}]

Final interview-ready answer

Render non-secret configuration from values into a ConfigMap and reference it in the Deployment as env or a volume. A checksum annotation on Pod templates can trigger a rollout when config changes. Do not put passwords in ConfigMaps.

050How do you manage secrets in Helm charts?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev get secret orders-db -o name
Existing Secret reference (container fragment)
env:
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: orders-db
        key: password

Final interview-ready answer

Store secrets in an approved secret manager and use an operator or pre-created Kubernetes Secret. Templates reference existingSecret names and keys, not plaintext. Helm release storage and rendered YAML can expose values, so --set or ignored files alone are insufficient.

051How do you configure resource requests, limits and health probes through values?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev describe pod POD
kubectl -n orders-dev top pods
Container resources and readiness fragment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "orders.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        {{- include "orders.selectorLabels" . | nindent 8 }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: orders-api
          {{- if .Values.image.digest }}
          image: {{ printf "%s@%s" .Values.image.repository .Values.image.digest | quote }}
          {{- else }}
          image: {{ printf "%s:%s" .Values.image.repository .Values.image.tag | quote }}
          {{- end }}
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: {{ .Values.containerPort }}
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: {{ .Values.healthPath | quote }}
              port: http
          resources:
            {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}

Final interview-ready answer

Set requests and limits in values, render them into the container spec, and configure startup/readiness/liveness probes for the real application endpoints. Readiness controls traffic eligibility; liveness can restart containers. Test settings under expected load.

052How do you configure HPA, affinity, tolerations and node selectors?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev get hpa
kubectl get nodes --show-labels
HPA example (requires metrics API and CPU requests)
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 5
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70

Final interview-ready answer

Expose optional settings in chart values and render them conditionally. HPA needs suitable metrics and CPU requests for utilization scaling; node selectors and affinity need matching nodes, and tolerations do not guarantee scheduling. Avoid conflicting replica ownership with HPA.

Environments, dependencies and lifecycle — Intermediate

053How do you manage Dev, QA and Production with Helm?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

SettingDevProd
Replicas24
Hostorders-dev.example.comorders.example.com
ImageSame approved digestSame approved digest

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml
helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-prod.yaml
Dev overrides
replicaCount: 2
ingress:
  enabled: true

Production overrides
replicaCount: 4

Use a shared versioned chart and explicit non-secret values files for each environment. Dev might use two replicas and prod four, while the same immutable image is promoted. Use distinct namespaces or clusters and check context before deploying.

054What are Helm dependencies and subcharts?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm dependency list ./orders-api
helm dependency update ./orders-api
Dependency declaration example (use actual approved version and URL)
dependencies:
  - name: redis
    version: "20.0.0"
    repository: https://charts.example.com
    condition: redis.enabled

Final interview-ready answer

A parent chart can declare versioned dependencies in Chart.yaml; dependency archives are placed in charts/. A subchart renders with its own values scope and parent overrides under its name. Use compatible versions and avoid bundling persistent dependencies blindly. Helm 2 requirements.yaml is covered with Chart.lock in the next question.

055What is the difference between helm dependency update and build? What is Chart.lock?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

CommandBehavior
dependency updateResolve and update lock
dependency buildRebuild from lock if present

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm dependency update ./orders-api
helm dependency build ./orders-api

Final interview-ready answer

update resolves versions from Chart.yaml, downloads them and records a lock file. build reconstructs dependencies from Chart.lock when present. Commit reviewed lock files and use build in CI for reproducibility. Helm 2 used requirements.yaml for dependencies.

056How do you pass values to subcharts and use global values?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm show values ./orders-api
helm template orders ./orders-api --debug
Parent values fragment
redis:
  enabled: true
global:
  environment: dev

Final interview-ready answer

Use the dependency name or alias as the parent values key. A subchart sees its own scoped values; global values can be shared by parent and subcharts. Avoid secret data in globals and check the dependency's documented values schema.

057What is an umbrella chart? When should dependencies be separate releases?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

AspectUmbrellaSeparate releases
LifecycleCoupledIndependent
Blast radiusLargerSmaller

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm dependency list ./orders-stack
helm list -A

Final interview-ready answer

An umbrella chart packages several charts under one release lifecycle. Separate releases isolate upgrades, ownership and recovery, which is often better for databases or independently released services. App of Apps is an Argo CD pattern, not an umbrella chart feature.

058What is a Helm library chart?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm show chart ./common
helm dependency build ./orders-api
Library Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: common
type: library
version: 1.0.0

Final interview-ready answer

A chart with type library contains reusable helper templates and is not installed as an application itself. Teams can share labels, probes and deployment templates through versioned library dependencies. Pin the library version and test consuming charts.

059What are Helm hooks and when do they run?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev get jobs
helm get hooks orders -n orders-dev
Hook annotations (Job metadata fragment)
annotations:
  helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade
  helm.sh/hook-weight: "-1"
  helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded

Final interview-ready answer

Hooks are annotated resources executed at lifecycle points such as pre-install, post-install, pre-upgrade and post-upgrade. Jobs can run migrations or tests. Hook weight controls ordering, and delete policies or TTL manage cleanup. Argo CD maps only supported hooks differently.

060How do you manage CRDs with Helm?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl get crd
helm show crds ./orders-api

Final interview-ready answer

Helm 3 installs missing static CRDs from crds/ before regular templates on installation. It does not routinely upgrade or delete those CRDs. Plan CRD lifecycle independently and verify compatibility before applying custom resources. Never delete a shared CRD just to fix a release.

Packaging, CI validation and GitOps — Intermediate

061How do you package and version a Helm chart?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm lint ./orders-api
helm package ./orders-api --destination dist

Final interview-ready answer

Update Chart.yaml version using SemVer when packaging changes, lint and package the chart as a tgz. appVersion is informational; ensure the image is explicitly pinned. Publish immutable artifacts and do not overwrite a version already consumed by teams.

062How do you publish charts to an HTTP repository?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm package ./orders-api --destination dist
helm repo index dist --url https://charts.example.com

Final interview-ready answer

Package chart archives, generate or merge index.yaml and publish archives plus index together using a controlled process. Use a trusted HTTPS repository and scoped credentials. Clients add the repo and pin the required chart version.

063How do you publish and install a Helm chart from Amazon ECR OCI?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

ArtifactDocker imageHelm OCI chart
ConsumerKubeletHelm / Argo CD
ContentsContainer layersChart package

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | helm registry login --username AWS --password-stdin 123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
ECR OCI commands (replace account; approved repository creation only)
REGISTRY=123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
aws ecr describe-repositories --repository-names charts/orders-api --region ap-south-1
# For this chart name, use an ECR repository charts/orders-api:
aws ecr create-repository --repository-name charts/orders-api --region ap-south-1
aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | helm registry login --username AWS --password-stdin "$REGISTRY"
helm package ./orders-api --destination dist
helm push dist/orders-api-1.0.0.tgz oci://$REGISTRY/charts
helm show chart oci://$REGISTRY/charts/orders-api --version 1.0.0
# Install only in a separate namespace not managed by Argo CD:
helm install orders oci://$REGISTRY/charts/orders-api --version 1.0.0 -n orders-oci --create-namespace

Final interview-ready answer

Create the chart repository in ECR, authenticate Helm to the registry and push the packaged chart to the parent OCI path. The archive name determines the final repository basename. OCI charts do not use an index.yaml or repo add.

064How do you sign and verify Helm charts?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm package --sign --key KEY_NAME --keyring KEYRING ./orders-api
helm verify orders-api-1.0.0.tgz --keyring TRUSTED_KEYRING

Final interview-ready answer

Use Helm provenance with a trusted GPG key to sign an archive and verify its signature and digest before installing. OCI signature tooling can be added according to policy. Signature verification proves integrity and signer trust, not that workloads are safe. Use least privilege, admission policy checks, approved repository access and signed chart verification. Do not treat signing as automatic admission enforcement.

065What is helm diff and why use it in CI/CD?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm plugin list
helm diff upgrade orders ./orders-api -n orders-dev -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml

Final interview-ready answer

helm-diff is an optional plugin, not a built-in Helm command. It previews changes before upgrading, so reviewers can identify risky changes and deletions. Install an approved pinned plugin and avoid exposing Secret values in output.

066How do you validate Helm charts before deployment?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm lint ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml
helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml > rendered.yaml
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -n orders-dev -f rendered.yaml

Final interview-ready answer

I lint the chart, render with actual environment inputs, validate manifest schemas and policies, then use server dry-run and a test deployment where appropriate. No single check proves readiness. Keep generated Secret data out of shared logs. Include chart-testing in CI, render with kubeconform or server dry-run, and run tests on an isolated cluster.

067What is helm test and how do you test charts in CI?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm test orders -n orders-dev --logs
kubectl -n orders-dev get jobs
templates/tests/health.yaml (requires image access and actual health endpoint)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: {{ include "orders.name" . }}-test
  annotations:
    helm.sh/hook: test
    helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: check
      image: curlimages/curl:8.12.1
      args:
        - "-fsS"
        - {{ printf "http://%s:%v%s" (include "orders.name" .) .Values.service.port .Values.healthPath | quote }}

Final interview-ready answer

helm test runs resources annotated with helm.sh/hook: test after a release is installed. CI can also use chart-testing, kubeconform, kind and application smoke tests. A test Job should fail with nonzero exit when service health fails.

068How do you use --wait, --timeout and --atomic safely?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

Flag (Helm 3)Purpose
--waitWait for supported readiness
--timeoutOperation wait limit
--atomicAttempt failure recovery
--wait-for-jobsWait for regular Jobs

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm upgrade --install orders ./orders-api -n orders-dev -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --atomic --wait --timeout 5m

Final interview-ready answer

In Helm 3, --wait waits for supported resources to become ready within --timeout. --wait-for-jobs adds regular Job completion, and --atomic attempts rollback on upgrade failure or cleanup on install failure. These do not undo external side effects. Helm 4 uses version-specific flags; check help.

069How do you use Helm in CI/CD pipelines?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm lint ./orders-api
helm upgrade --install orders ./orders-api -n orders-dev -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --wait

Final interview-ready answer

CI builds, tests and scans an image, pushes it to a registry, validates the chart and uses an approved deploy identity. Direct CD runs Helm; GitOps CD updates Git and lets Argo CD sync. Use one owner per workload and verify health after deployment.

070How do you configure Argo CD to deploy a Helm chart?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

Application fieldExampleMeaning

source.pathcharts/orders-apiChart directory

helm.valueFilesvalues-dev.yamlRelative values file

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
argocd app get orders-dev
argocd app manifests orders-dev
applications/orders-dev.yaml

kind: Application
metadata:
  name: orders-dev
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default # Lab only; use a restricted project in production
  source:

An Application points at the Git chart path or a chart repository, revision and destination. source.helm.valueFiles selects environment values. Argo CD renders Helm templates and applies them; it does not create a normal Helm release history. Rollback changes Git.

Real project requirements and automation — Advanced

071How many charts and microservices do you maintain? What charts already exist?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
find charts -name Chart.yaml
helm list -A

Final interview-ready answer

Use actual counts. An illustrative project has orders-api, payments-api and frontend application charts, a common library chart and separately managed monitoring and ingress components. Each chart has an owner, documented inputs and independent versioning. Report your actual Helm version and cluster count; verify with helm version and kubectl config get-contexts.

072How do requirements for a new Helm chart come to your DevOps team?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
git switch -c feature/OPS-142-orders-chart

Final interview-ready answer

A Jira request usually provides service name, source repo, image, environment and acceptance criteria. I clarify missing details, reuse the team chart if suitable, create a feature branch and open a PR for review. I do not assume a service port or production resources. Collect port, health endpoint, image digest, replicas, resource limits, storage, secrets, network policy and target namespace before writing templates.

073Where do you maintain Helm charts, values and Argo CD Application files?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
git ls-files '*Chart.yaml' '*values*.yaml' '*application*.yaml'
Repository layout
platform-gitops/
├── charts/
│   └── orders-api/
│       ├── Chart.yaml
│       ├── values.yaml
│       ├── values-dev.yaml
│       ├── values-qa.yaml
│       ├── values-prod.yaml
│       ├── values.schema.json

    └── orders-prod.yaml

Final interview-ready answer

Keep application code and Dockerfile in an app repo, reusable chart source in a chart repo or GitOps repo, and reviewed environment values/Application definitions in GitOps Git. Publish chart packages to ECR OCI if needed. Ownership and version references must be clear.

074A developer requests a new Spring Boot microservice. How do you turn the request into a chart and deployment?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm lint ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml
helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml
Jira example — illustrative
OPS-142: Deploy orders-api in Dev
Application port: 8080
Health: /actuator/health
Replicas: 2
Service: ClusterIP, port 80
Ingress: orders-dev.example.com
Acceptance: rollout complete, ready endpoints, HTTP 200
Change: reviewed PR, approved image, deployment evidence
Terminal · image build and publish (requires Maven artifact, Dockerfile and existing ECR image repository)
REGISTRY=123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
TAG=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
mvn clean package
docker build -t "$REGISTRY/orders-api:$TAG" .
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL "$REGISTRY/orders-api:$TAG"
aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin "$REGISTRY"
docker push "$REGISTRY/orders-api:$TAG"
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name orders-api --image-ids imageTag="$TAG" --region ap-south-1 --query 'imageDetails[0].imageDigest' --output text
# Commit digest into image.digest in reviewed environment values.

Final interview-ready answer

For the sample orders-api, I agree on port 8080, /actuator/health, two dev replicas, image reference and hostname. I create Chart.yaml, values and resource templates with matching selectors, review rendered YAML, deploy to dev and verify the URL. Promote via reviewed changes only. Build and scan the application image before updating the chart. Push to ECR using a scoped identity and verify its digest.

075Can you write a Jenkins pipeline to validate and deploy a Helm chart?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm lint ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml
helm upgrade --install orders ./orders-api -n orders-dev -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --wait
Jenkinsfile · direct Helm lab
pipeline {
  agent { label 'trusted-helm-aws' }
  options { disableConcurrentBuilds() }
  stages {
    stage('Validate') {
      steps {
        sh 'helm lint ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml'
        sh 'helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml > rendered.yaml'
      }
    }
    stage('Deploy Dev') {
      steps {
        input message: 'Deploy reviewed chart to Dev?'
        sh '''set -eu
aws eks update-kubeconfig --region ap-south-1 --name demo-eks
helm upgrade --install orders ./orders-api -n orders-dev --create-namespace -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --atomic --timeout 5m
kubectl -n orders-dev rollout status deployment/orders --timeout=5m
'''
      }
    }
  }
}

Final interview-ready answer

Use a trusted agent with Helm, AWS CLI and kubectl. Checkout reviewed code, lint/render, review diff, require approval for prod and deploy with scoped permissions. Archive non-secret validation reports and verify rollout and health. In GitOps mode, replace helm upgrade with a PR to GitOps.

076How do you use GitHub Actions to package and publish a chart?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm package ./orders-api --destination dist
helm push dist/orders-api-1.0.0.tgz oci://123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
GitHub Actions deployment job fragment — trusted runner, preconfigured scoped AWS identity
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, trusted-helm-aws]
    environment: chart-publish
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4 # Pin a reviewed full SHA in production
      - name: Validate and publish
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          REGISTRY=123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
          helm lint ./orders-api
          helm package ./orders-api --destination dist
          aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | helm registry login --username AWS --password-stdin "$REGISTRY"
          helm push dist/orders-api-1.0.0.tgz oci://$REGISTRY/charts
# Requires chart repository charts/orders-api and trusted AWS role.
# For hosted runners configure scoped OIDC before registry login.

Final interview-ready answer

Use a protected workflow with scoped AWS OIDC credentials, pinned actions, chart version checks, lint and packaging. Authenticate to ECR OCI and publish only from approved branches or tags. Do not publish from untrusted pull requests. OCI chart repositories and container image repositories are distinct artifacts even when they share a registry.

077How do you promote the same image and chart across Dev, QA and Prod?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm show chart ./orders-api
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name orders-api --region ap-south-1

Final interview-ready answer

Build once, record chart version and image digest, validate in dev and promote the same artifacts through approved environment values changes. Only environment-specific replicas, hosts and config should differ. Keep the promotion history in Git.

078How do you safely upgrade production charts and handle breaking changes?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm history orders -n orders-prod
helm diff upgrade orders ./orders-api -n orders-prod -f ./orders-api/values-prod.yaml

Final interview-ready answer

Review version changes and rendered diffs, check immutable fields and Kubernetes compatibility, test on staging and plan migrations. Approve the exact versions, deploy in a maintenance window when needed, monitor health and retain a recovery path. Do not assume rollback reverses data changes.

079How do you handle database schema migrations with Helm?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev get jobs
kubectl -n orders-dev logs job/MIGRATION_JOB

Final interview-ready answer

Use a reviewed migration Job at the correct lifecycle point, with bounded retries and idempotent or repeat-safe logic. Coordinate backups and backward-compatible schema changes using expand/contract. Helm rollback cannot restore database data or undo migrations automatically.

080How do you implement rolling, blue-green and canary deployments with Helm?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

StrategyBehavior
RollingReplace Pods gradually
Blue-greenSwitch active traffic target
CanaryGradually increase traffic share

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev rollout status deployment/orders
kubectl -n orders-dev get rollouts

Final interview-ready answer

Helm renders deployment or rollout manifests; Kubernetes and controllers implement strategies. A rolling Deployment uses surge and availability settings; blue-green or canary typically uses Argo Rollouts or a traffic manager. Validate readiness and monitor traffic before promotion.

Production troubleshooting — Advanced

081How do you deploy the same chart across multiple clusters and clouds?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl config get-contexts
helm list --kube-context demo-dev -A

Final interview-ready answer

Use distinct kubeconfigs or Argo CD Applications with per-cluster values for ingress, storage, IAM and secrets. Pin the same chart and image, test cluster-specific differences and enforce approval boundaries. Avoid a single uncontrolled loop updating all production clusters.

082How do you monitor Helm release and application health?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm status orders -n orders-dev
kubectl -n orders-dev get pods
kubectl -n orders-dev get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

Final interview-ready answer

Helm status and history describe release operations, while kubectl and Prometheus/Grafana report runtime health, readiness, errors and latency. Monitor alerts and correlate versions with incidents. Use Argo CD for continuous drift detection if it owns the workload.

083Helm template fails with nil pointer or invalid YAML. How do you fix it?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm lint ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml
helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml --debug

Investigation sequence

  1. Render error
  2. Identify template
  3. Check scope / values
  4. Fix
  5. Render again

Final interview-ready answer

Render with the exact CI values, use --debug and isolate the failing template using --show-only where possible. Check nested keys, scope, indentation and types. Add schema or required checks rather than masking every error with defaults.

084Helm chart dependencies are missing or cannot be downloaded. What do you check?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm dependency list ./orders-api
helm dependency build ./orders-api

Investigation sequence

  1. Dependency declaration
  2. Lock
  3. Repository access
  4. Download
  5. Render

Final interview-ready answer

Inspect Chart.yaml, Chart.lock and charts/. Verify repo URL, version availability, credentials and network/TLS. Use dependency build with a reviewed lock file, or update intentionally and review lock changes. Avoid silently upgrading dependencies in production.

085Helm install fails with resource already exists or ownership metadata errors. How do you recover?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev get svc orders -o yaml
helm list -A

Investigation sequence

  1. Existing object
  2. Identify owner
  3. Choose safe ownership plan
  4. Retry

Final interview-ready answer

Inspect the existing object's owner labels and annotations and identify its current manager. Decide whether to rename the release, keep the resource external or plan an approved adoption. Never delete shared resources or force ownership without backup and coordination.

086Helm install or upgrade fails due to missing or conflicting CRDs. How do you fix it?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl get crd
kubectl wait --for=condition=Established crd/EXAMPLE_CRD --timeout=60s

Investigation sequence

  1. Missing CRD
  2. Supported CRD install
  3. Established
  4. Custom resources

Final interview-ready answer

Check CRD existence, served versions, operator readiness and ownership. Install or upgrade CRDs using the operator's supported process and wait until established before applying custom resources. Do not use skip-crds unless compatible CRDs already exist.

087Helm upgrade fails due to an immutable field. How do you handle it?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev get deploy orders -o yaml
helm template orders ./orders-api

Investigation sequence

  1. API rejects field
  2. Compare old and new
  3. Plan migration
  4. Verify

Final interview-ready answer

Identify the exact immutable field from the API error, often a Deployment selector or Service field. Preserve stable identifiers where possible. If replacement is required, design a new resource and traffic migration, validate data retention and get approval. Force replacement can cause downtime.

088Helm release is stuck PendingInstall or PendingUpgrade. How do you troubleshoot?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm history orders -n orders-dev
helm status orders -n orders-dev
kubectl -n orders-dev get jobs,pods

Investigation sequence

  1. Pending release
  2. Active operation?
  3. Hooks / events
  4. Coordinated recovery

Final interview-ready answer

Separate Helm operation status from Pod Pending state. Inspect history, active CI jobs, hooks and Kubernetes events; identify whether an operation still runs or timed out. Stop concurrent writers, then use a supported recovery or rollback only after confirming no operation is active.

089Helm deployment fails because pods are Pending or quotas are exceeded. What do you do?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev describe pod POD
kubectl -n orders-dev get resourcequota,pvc
kubectl get nodes

Investigation sequence

  1. Pending Pod
  2. Scheduler events
  3. Capacity / PVC / constraints
  4. Fix

Final interview-ready answer

Describe the Pod and inspect scheduler events, resource requests, quotas, PVC binding, affinity and taints. Fix incorrect values or obtain approved capacity/quota changes. Retest scheduling and application readiness rather than arbitrarily lowering resource limits.

090Helm deployment fails with ImagePullBackOff. How do you fix it?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev describe pod POD
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name orders-api --region ap-south-1

Investigation sequence

  1. Pod event
  2. Image reference
  3. Registry access
  4. Pull succeeds

Final interview-ready answer

Check the rendered image reference, whether the image exists and node or Fargate execution role ECR permissions, networking and registry credentials. For generic registries, check namespace-local imagePullSecrets. Helm renders the reference; kubelet pulls the image.

091Helm deployment fails with CrashLoopBackOff or failed probes. How do you troubleshoot?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev logs POD --previous
kubectl -n orders-dev describe pod POD

Investigation sequence

  1. Restarting Pod
  2. Logs / exit code
  3. Config / probes
  4. Fix
  5. Ready

Final interview-ready answer

Inspect previous container logs, exit code, events, config and resources. Check actual listen port and health endpoint, distinguish startup from readiness and liveness failures, fix the chart or application, and verify rollout. Do not disable probes just to show success.

092Helm deployment succeeds but the application URL is inaccessible. How do you troubleshoot?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl -n orders-dev get ingress,svc,endpointslices
dig orders-dev.example.com
curl -v https://orders-dev.example.com

Investigation sequence

  1. DNS
  2. Load balancer
  3. Ingress
  4. Service
  5. Ready endpoints
  6. App

Final interview-ready answer

Start with DNS and load balancer, check ingress controller and ingressClass, backend service name and port, EndpointSlices and pod readiness. Port-forward the Service and test HTTP to isolate internal application failure. Inspect network policies and TLS as needed.

093Helm installation fails because a namespace or Secret is missing. What do you check?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
kubectl get ns orders-dev
kubectl -n orders-dev get secret orders-db -o name

Investigation sequence

  1. Namespace
  2. External secret ready
  3. Workload reference
  4. Pod starts

Final interview-ready answer

Confirm namespace, context, RBAC and required existing Secret names. --create-namespace can create the release namespace during install, but it does not create external secrets or other namespaces automatically. Arrange secret operator readiness before workloads or hooks use them.

094A Helm hook Job fails during upgrade. How do you recover?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm get hooks orders -n orders-dev
kubectl -n orders-dev get jobs
kubectl -n orders-dev logs job/MIGRATION_JOB

Investigation sequence

  1. Hook failure
  2. Job logs
  3. Check side effects
  4. Fix
  5. Controlled retry

Final interview-ready answer

Inspect Job status, logs, events, hook annotations and required credentials or dependencies. Understand whether migration side effects occurred before retrying. Fix the cause and use a safe approved recovery plan; hook Jobs are not always cleaned up automatically.

095A Helm upgrade partially succeeds and production is broken. How do you roll back safely?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm history orders -n orders-prod
helm rollback orders REVISION -n orders-prod --wait --timeout 5m

Investigation sequence

  1. Incident
  2. Freeze changes
  3. Known-good revision / Git
  4. Recover
  5. Verify

Final interview-ready answer

Stop additional deployments, identify the last known-good revision and inspect current resources and migration state. With direct Helm ownership, roll back after assessing data compatibility; with Argo CD ownership, revert Git. Confirm rollout, endpoint health and error rates before closing the incident. General failure triage starts with helm status, helm get values -a, helm get manifest, kubectl describe and events.

096A Helm chart works locally but fails in staging or CI. How do you investigate?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm version
kubectl config current-context
helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-qa.yaml --debug

Investigation sequence

  1. Local vs CI inputs
  2. Render compare
  3. Cluster differences
  4. Fix

Final interview-ready answer

Reproduce the exact chart version, dependency lock, Helm version and override order. Check context, Kubernetes API versions, permissions, quota, secrets, network and admission rules. Local rendering cannot prove cluster compatibility. Fix the difference in reviewed code.

097Someone manually edits a Helm-managed Deployment. What happens?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

Direct HelmArgo CD
Drift not continuously reconciledDrift detected automatically
Reviewed upgrade to reconcileSync / optional self-heal

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm get manifest orders -n orders-dev
kubectl -n orders-dev get deploy orders -o yaml

Investigation sequence

  1. Manual edit
  2. Live drift
  3. Direct Helm: next operation; Manual edit
  4. Argo CD: detect / optional self-heal

Final interview-ready answer

Direct Helm does not continuously reconcile live drift. Inspect live state against the rendered release and coordinate a reviewed upgrade to restore intended fields. Argo CD may detect and self-heal drift when configured. Avoid using force as a routine fix.

098Argo CD deploys a Helm chart but helm list shows nothing. Why?

Side-by-side comparison / field guide

Direct HelmArgo CD Helm rendering
helm list contains releaseNo conventional Helm release
helm rollbackGit revert / sync

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm list -n orders-dev
argocd app get orders-dev
argocd app manifests orders-dev

Investigation sequence

  1. Helm chart
  2. Argo CD render
  3. Kubernetes resources; Direct Helm install
  4. Release record

Final interview-ready answer

Argo CD uses Helm for template generation and applies the resources through its own controller. It does not normally create Helm release Secrets or release revisions. Inspect Argo CD Application status and Git history, and do not install the same chart directly to fix the empty list.

GitOps operations and architecture — Advanced

099Argo CD Helm Application is OutOfSync or fails to render. How do you fix it?

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
argocd app get orders-dev --hard-refresh
argocd app diff orders-dev
kubectl -n argocd logs deploy/argocd-repo-server --tail=100

Investigation sequence

  1. Application error
  2. Source / values
  3. Render
  4. Diff
  5. Git fix
  6. Sync

Final interview-ready answer

Check source revision, chart path, valueFiles, repo authentication, dependencies and repo-server errors. Compare desired and live manifests; avoid random template values that change each render. Fix source in Git, refresh and sync only after reviewing changes.

100Explain the complete real-time Helm and Argo CD project architecture.

Practical commands

Terminal · examples (replace placeholders and confirm context)
helm template orders ./orders-api -f ./orders-api/values-dev.yaml
argocd app get orders-dev
kubectl -n orders-dev get deploy,svc,ingress,endpointslices

Final interview-ready answer

A Jira request defines the service requirements. CI builds and scans the orders-api image and pushes it to ECR. A reviewed chart contains reusable Deployment, Service and Ingress templates. Environment values select image digest, replicas, resources and hostname. Direct Helm is one deployment option; in GitOps, Argo CD reads the approved chart and values from Git, renders and syncs to EKS. Kubernetes schedules Pods and pulls ECR images. User traffic follows the ingress data plane to ready Pods. Monitor health, promote immutable artifacts and recover via Git revert for GitOps or Helm rollback for direct releases.

Reference documentation and assumptions

Based on the supplied Helm training guide (25 questions) and additional 100-question bank. Duplicate concepts were consolidated; examples were expanded. Corrections include release history on uninstall, computed values, CRD lifecycle, secret handling and the distinction between Argo CD and direct Helm ownership. The main syntax targets Helm 3; check Helm 4 documentation for changed flags. See Helm 3 usage, Helm upgrade, chart structure, Helm 4 upgrade reference, Argo CD Helm integration and ECR OCI charts. Example domains, account IDs, versions and project counts are illustrative. Commands are not executed; test in an isolated cluster before production. Use approved credentials, backup plans and change controls.
